title: Burden and impact of infections among adult liver transplantation-related hospitalizations: A nationwide analysis
content:
by Sahiljot Singh Bhupal, Joseph Solomon, Saniya Jiwani, Carol Singh, Aalam Sohal, Mohanad Al-Qaisi, Nilofar Najafian

Introduction

The presence of infections in patients undergoing liver transplantation (LT) has been associated with worsened clinical outcomes. We aimed to examine the current burden and impact of infections during index LT hospitalization using a large national cohort.

Methods

We analyzed data from the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) Database (2016–2022) to identify all hospitalizations for LT aged >18. Hospitalizations were stratified into two groups based on infection status. Data collected included patient demographics, liver disease etiology, liver-related decompensations, comorbidities, and clinical outcomes. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate categorical outcomes, and survey-weighted generalized linear models with a gamma distribution and log link were used to evaluate length of stay and hospitalization costs.

Results

Among the 50,630 hospitalizations for LT, 15,130 (29.9%) had infections. The most common infections observed were pneumonia (8.5%), urinary tract infections (UTI) (8.3%), and cholangitis (7.5%). After adjusting for confounding factors, hospitalizations with infections had a higher odds of all cause mortality (aOR-1.47, 95% CI-1.14–1.90, p = 0.003), non-home discharges (aOR-1.89, 95% CI-1.70–2.10, p < 0.001), total complications (aOR-1.65, 95% CI-1.49–1.82, p < 0.001), longer adjusted predicted length of stay (30 days vs 16.2 days) and higher adjusted predicted hospitalization cost ($235,953 vs $156,336).

Conclusion

Infections in hospitalizations for LT were associated with higher morbidity and greater resource utilization. These findings highlight the need for targeted preventive strategies in this patient population.
